strengths: First promptable 3D part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data (rather than lifting 2D SAM masks), directly addressing a well-motivated limitation of prior clustering-based and 2D-lifting methods, notably enabling segmentation of interior/occluded structures that surface-based methods (PartField, SAMPart3D) miss.

The dual-branch encoder design is a sensible engineering solution to the practical problem of not being able to directly train a SAM-like decoder with incomplete 2D-derived masks, while retaining useful pretrained priors from PartField/SAM; ablations (Table 3) support the value of this design over single-branch alternatives.

The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline for mining 5M+ shape-part pairs from noisy/fragmented artist assets is a creative and practically useful data curation contribution, and the visualization (Fig. 10) provides some transparency into how filtering works.

Strong quantitative improvements over relevant baselines (Point-SAM, PartField, SAMPart3D, SAMesh, PartSLIP, Find3D) across interactive and automatic segmentation on multiple benchmarks, with reasonably careful experimental design (e.g., disabling mesh connectivity for PartField to avoid label leakage, Table 4 analysis).
Reasonable complexity/efficiency analysis showing feed-forward inference is much faster than optimization-based lifting methods and only marginally slower than PartField.

Ablations isolate the contribution of both architecture and data scale in a clear, informative way, and additional applications (interior part editing, amodal segmentation via HoloPart) suggest practical utility beyond the core benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: No code/model release at submission time ('will be released soon'), and given the heavy reliance on curated proprietary-style data pipelines (Objaverse mining, model-in-the-loop filtering thresholds like IoU@1>60 or IoU@10>90), reproducibility is a real concern; the exact thresholds/hyperparameters seem somewhat ad hoc without justification or sensitivity analysis.

Quantitative evaluation of 'internal structure' segmentation claims (a central motivating example, Fig. 2) is only shown qualitatively; there is no benchmark or quantitative metric specifically targeting interior-part accuracy to substantiate the claimed advantage over PartField/SAMPart3D beyond a single illustrative example.

The automatic segmentation ('Segment Every Part') evaluation protocol reports the best score across multiple NMS thresholds for PartSAM while other multi-scale baselines are also given their best score, but the paper does not report variance/robustness of PartSAM across granularities, nor how a practitioner would choose the threshold at inference without ground truth — this undercuts the 'automatic' framing somewhat.
The semantic labeling limitation (masks are unlabeled, as in 2D SAM) restricts direct usability for tasks needing categorical part names, and the proposed future fix is only sketched, not attempted.

Training data curation heavily depends on Objaverse and licensed datasets, plus PartField pseudo-labels; the potential bias/error propagation from PartField (a baseline being compared against) into PartSAM's supervision could confound the comparison, and this circularity (using a competitor model to generate training pseudo-labels, then beating that competitor) is not thoroughly discussed or controlled for.
No discussion of failure cases or robustness to noisy/low-quality real-world scans versus clean artist/AI-generated meshes, limiting insight into generalization boundaries.

Statistical significance / variance across runs is not reported for the main quantitative comparisons, and dataset sizes (e.g., PartObjaverse-Tiny) are quite small, raising some concern about the robustness of reported margins.

strengths: Addresses a genuine limitation of prior 2D-lifting approaches (surface-only understanding, lack of interior structure segmentation) with clear qualitative evidence (Fig. 2, Fig. 6) that PartSAM can segment occluded/interior geometry that SAM-lifting methods cannot.

Strong and consistent quantitative improvements over multiple recent baselines (Point-SAM, PartField, SAMPart3D, SAMesh, Find3D, PartSLIP) across both interactive (Table 1) and automatic segmentation (Table 2) protocols, with large margins (e.g., >90% relative gain at single-click prompting).

The model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline is a clever and non-trivial solution for scaling native 3D part supervision beyond the small set of well-structured artist meshes, expanding coverage from ~180k to ~500k shapes / 5M parts.

Careful, self-critical evaluation methodology: the authors identify and correct a potential label-leakage issue in the standard PartObjaverse-Tiny protocol (mesh connectivity correlating with ground truth) and re-evaluate baselines fairly (Section 4.2, A.2.4), which is a commendable level of rigor often missing in related work.

Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contributions of the encoder design (dual-branch vs. point-based vs. frozen/learnable PartField) and the training data stages, which support the paper's core claims about architecture and data scaling being complementary.

Practical downstream demonstrations (interior part editing, amodal segmentation via HoloPart) and a complexity/runtime analysis versus optimization-based baselines add some evidence of real-world usefulness.
weaknesses: The 'native 3D, not reliant on 2D' framing is partially undercut by the architecture itself: one encoder branch is initialized from and frozen at PartField weights, which were originally learned via contrastive distillation from SAM's 2D masks. The claimed conceptual separation from 2D-derived priors is therefore not as clean as the abstract/intro suggest.

The large-scale model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is fundamentally bootstrapped from PartField pseudo-labels (multi-scale clustering outputs), the very method the paper positions as inferior; the filtering thresholds (IoU@1>60 or IoU@10>90, >5 valid masks per shape) are heuristic and not justified or ablated for sensitivity, raising concerns about how much of PartSAM's improvement is really independent of PartField's segmentation style versus refined/relabeled from it.

No code or model checkpoints are currently available ("will be released soon"), which limits reproducibility for a paper making strong scaling and data-curation claims that are difficult to verify without access to the curated dataset or pipeline scripts.

Quantitative evaluation is limited to two benchmarks (PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNetE); broader coverage (e.g., full PartNet categories, more diverse AI-generated mesh benchmarks with ground truth, or held-out categories testing true open-world generalization) would strengthen claims of general-purpose foundation-model behavior.

No semantic labels are produced (acknowledged limitation), which meaningfully constrains applicability compared to systems that combine segmentation with semantics; this is left as future work without any concrete experiments.

Results are reported as single numbers without variance/multiple seeds, and there is limited failure-case analysis or discussion of when/why PartSAM's segmentation still fails (e.g., on extremely thin or highly ambiguous parts).

Minor writing/clarity issues remain (e.g., "duan-branch" typo), and some architectural/training details (e.g., choice of triplane resolution, patch count, prompt sampling within bottom-third distance) are presented without ablation or justification for these specific design choices.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of prior 2D-lifting approaches to 3D part segmentation (surface-only understanding, lack of interior structure, uncontrolled clustering-based decomposition) with a native 3D training paradigm.

Strong quantitative results: large margins over Point-SAM (interactive) and SAMesh/SAMPart3D/PartField/PartSLIP/Find3D (automatic) across PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNet-E, with qualitative examples supporting the claims (e.g., interior leg/knee segmentation, grenade body, AI-generated meshes).

Thoughtful dual-branch encoder design (frozen PartField branch + learnable branch) is empirically justified via ablation, showing it avoids catastrophic forgetting of 2D-distilled SAM priors while still scaling to native 3D supervision.

Model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is a practical and scalable solution to bootstrap labels for highly fragmented artist meshes, expanding training data from 180k/2M to 500k shapes/5M parts; qualitative examples (Fig. 10) show sensible filtering behavior.

The paper proactively identifies and corrects an evaluation fairness issue (mesh-connectivity label leakage in PartObjaverse-Tiny for PartField), which is a good sign of scientific rigor, and includes a fair re-evaluation in the appendix.
Reasonable complexity/efficiency analysis versus optimization-based baselines (SAMesh, SAMPart3D) showing large speed advantages while remaining competitive in runtime with PartField.
Demonstrates useful downstream applications (interior part editing, amodal part segmentation via HoloPart integration) that showcase practical value beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: Novelty of the core architecture is somewhat incremental: the encoder's frozen branch is directly initialized from PartField's pretrained weights, meaning the method's 3D priors are still partially bootstrapped from a model that was itself trained via SAM-distilled contrastive learning, which slightly undercuts the framing of a fully 'native' 3D approach.

The model-in-the-loop annotation criteria (IoU@1 > 60 or IoU@10 > 90, >5 valid masks per shape) are heuristic thresholds without ablation or sensitivity analysis showing how robust results are to these choices.

Interactive segmentation comparison (Table 1) only includes Point-SAM as a baseline; stronger or more diverse baselines (e.g., Find3D, iSeg) are not evaluated in the promptable setting, limiting the completeness of this comparison.

PartSAM cannot produce semantic labels for masks (acknowledged as a limitation), which restricts applicability for tasks requiring category-aware part understanding, a notable gap relative to some 2D-lifting competitors that do assign semantic labels.

No quantitative evaluation specifically targeting interior/occluded structure segmentation (the paper's core differentiator is largely demonstrated only qualitatively, e.g., Fig. 2 and Fig. 6, without a dedicated benchmark or metric for internal-part accuracy).

Reproducibility is limited at submission time since code and model weights are only promised for future release ('will be released soon'), and some data curation details (e.g., exact filtering thresholds for shape complexity, artist scene graph parsing heuristics) may be hard to reproduce precisely.
No variance/error bars or statistical significance analysis is reported for the quantitative comparisons, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported large margins.
Minor writing issues (e.g., typo 'duan-branch' in the introduction) suggest the manuscript could benefit from an additional proofreading pass.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in the literature: prior open-world 3D part segmentation methods rely on lifting 2D SAM masks (multi-view) into 3D, which causes surface-only understanding and inability to segment occluded/interior structures; this paper instead trains natively on 3D supervision, directly targeting this limitation with convincing qualitative examples (Fig. 2, 9).

The SAM-inspired promptable encoder-decoder design (as opposed to clustering-based segmentation used by PartField/SAMPart3D) provides explicit user controllability and avoids the need for manually tuned cluster numbers, which is a meaningful practical improvement.

The dual-branch encoder is a reasonable design choice that balances retention of pretrained 2D-distilled priors (frozen branch) with adaptation to native 3D supervision (learnable branch), and the ablations (Table 3) support that this design choice meaningfully outperforms naive fine-tuning or training-from-scratch variants.

The model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline is a creative and scalable solution to the noisy/fragmented mesh connectivity problem, expanding the corpus from ~180k to 500k shapes / 5M+ parts, and the paper provides a reasonably detailed description and validation (Fig. 15) of the filtering heuristic.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparisons on multiple benchmarks (PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNetE, 3DCoMPaT++) against several strong/recent baselines (Point-SAM, SAMesh, SAMPart3D, PartField, Find3D, PartSLIP), with large and consistent margins of improvement, plus thorough ablations, scaling curves, complexity analysis, cross-shape consistency evaluation, and failure-case analysis in the appendix.

The paper is careful about evaluation protocol issues, e.g., identifying and correcting for potential label leakage from mesh connectivity when comparing against PartField on PartObjaverse-Tiny, showing methodological rigor.
Demonstrated downstream applications (interior part editing, amodal part segmentation via HoloPart integration) show practical value beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The training data quality relies substantially on pseudo-labels generated by PartField itself (for the over-fragmented majority of assets), creating a degree of circularity: PartSAM's supervision inherits PartField's biases/failure modes for shapes lacking clean connectivity, and the claimed superiority of PartSAM's native 3D understanding is therefore partly bootstrapped from a 2D/clustering-based method rather than fully independent 3D ground truth.

No human verification or systematic quality audit of the curated 5M shape-part pairs is reported; the paper acknowledges 'a very small number of imperfect cases' but provides no quantitative estimate of annotation noise or its effect on downstream benchmarks.

Architecturally, the contribution is largely a careful combination of existing components (SAM's promptable encoder-decoder recipe, PartField's triplane feature-field encoder and pretrained weights, PVCNN, standard focal/dice/contrastive losses), which somewhat limits the technical novelty relative to the strong empirical gains reported.

Evaluation benchmarks (PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNetE) are relatively small and may not fully capture open-world diversity; robustness on larger/more diverse real-world or heavily out-of-distribution categories (e.g., scanned objects, as briefly touched on in the appendix) is less thoroughly quantified than the AI-generated/artist-mesh settings.

The model cannot produce semantic labels for segmented parts (acknowledged as future work), limiting immediate applicability for tasks that require semantic understanding rather than purely geometric part discovery.
The long-tail/rare-part limitation is acknowledged qualitatively (Fig. 14) but not quantitatively analyzed, leaving open how frequently and how severely this issue affects real deployment.

Reproducibility is not fully verifiable from the manuscript alone: it is unclear whether code, curated data, or model weights will be released, and the project page link is empty in the provided version, which affects the ability to independently validate the very large claimed performance margins.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of prior open-world 3D part segmentation work (reliance on 2D-lifted SAM masks), with a clear motivation illustrated by the failure of clustering-based methods (e.g., PartField) on interior/occluded structures.

The SAM-style promptable encoder-decoder design, applied natively to 3D via a triplane feature field, is a sensible and well-engineered adaptation that yields controllable, feed-forward interactive segmentation rather than relying on post-hoc clustering.

Large-scale data curation pipeline (model-in-the-loop filtering using interactive IoU criteria) is a reasonable automated strategy to scale 3D part supervision to millions of shape-part pairs without manual annotation.

Extensive empirical evaluation: interactive segmentation (vs. Point-SAM), automatic 'segment-every-part' comparisons against five baselines, hierarchical/multi-scale segmentation, cross-shape correspondence via functional maps, scaling curves, complexity analysis, and additional evaluation on 3DCoMPaT++.

Reported quantitative gains over baselines are large and consistent across datasets (PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNet-E, 3DCoMPaT++), and ablations isolate contributions of the dual-branch encoder, pretrained initialization, and the model-in-the-loop data stage.
Useful downstream applications demonstrated (interior part editing, amodal segmentation via HoloPart) showing practical relevance beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The 'native 3D' framing is somewhat overstated: the frozen encoder branch and both branches' initial weights come from PartField, whose own 2D-distilled/contrastive-trained priors are explicitly described as encoding 'rich 2D knowledge distilled from SAM.' Moreover, the second (larger) stage of training data is itself generated by filtering PartField's clustering outputs, so a large fraction of the 'native 3D' supervision is indirectly bootstrapped from a model with 2D-derived priors, which weakens the central novelty claim versus 2D-lifting approaches.

No manual verification or quality audit of the automatically curated 5M-part dataset; reliability rests entirely on heuristic IoU thresholds and shape-level filters, with only qualitative spot-checks (Fig. 15) provided as evidence of annotation quality.
Missing comparison to iSeg (Lang et al., 2024), a directly relevant interactive 3D segmentation method distilling SAM features, despite being discussed in related work.

The protocol change disabling mesh connectivity for PartField (to avoid 'label leakage') is a reasonable concern but introduces a non-standard evaluation setting; while the paper also reports connectivity-enabled results, the primary comparison table selectively favors the setting most unfavorable to the main competitor, which complicates fair assessment.

Reported improvements (e.g., 91% relative IoU@1 gain over Point-SAM) are very large; although an ablation retrains Point-SAM on the same curated data, the gap may still partly reflect architecture/capacity differences (118M vs. unspecified Point-SAM params) rather than purely the proposed native-3D design, and no error bars/statistical significance are reported.

Training/evaluation data is drawn almost entirely from Objaverse-derived sources (plus PartNet/ABO); generalization to truly out-of-distribution domains (e.g., real-world scans) is only shown qualitatively with visible failure cases (Fig. 18), not quantitatively benchmarked.
The model produces only class-agnostic masks without semantic labels, limiting its direct utility for many downstream tasks; this is acknowledged as a limitation but not addressed.

Claimed efficiency advantage over PartField is marginal (~12s vs ~10s per shape) despite the added architectural complexity (dual-branch encoder, decoder, multi-round interactive simulation), somewhat undercutting the 'scalable/efficient' framing.

Several components (prompt-guided mask decoder, IoU token, multi-mask ambiguity handling, interactive training simulation) are directly transplanted from SAM with limited fundamental innovation beyond adapting them to a triplane 3D representation.

strengths: First promptable 3D part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data (as opposed to lifting 2D SAM masks), addressing fundamental limitations of prior clustering-based and 2D-lifting approaches, including surface-only understanding and lack of controllability.

The dual-branch triplane encoder is a thoughtful design that balances scalability to native 3D supervision with retention of valuable 2D SAM priors distilled via PartField, and the ablations convincingly justify this design choice (showing frozen/learnable/no-pretrain variants all underperform).

The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is a creative and practical solution to the data scarcity problem, enabling scaling from 180k to 500k shapes and 5M+ parts, with clear validation of the filtering criteria via qualitative examples (Figure 15).

Extensive and convincing experimental validation: strong quantitative gains over Point-SAM (91% relative improvement with 1 prompt), large margins over SOTA on automatic/class-agnostic segmentation (>20% IoU improvement), and thorough ablations (architecture, training data, scaling curves).

Careful and fair experimental design, notably the identification and correction of a label-leakage issue in PartObjaverse-Tiny evaluation (mesh connectivity encoding ground truth), which is an important contribution to fair benchmarking in this subfield.

Good breadth of supplementary analyses: complexity/runtime analysis, cross-shape consistency via functional maps, additional dataset (3DCoMPaT++), and applications (interior part editing, amodal segmentation combined with HoloPart) that demonstrate practical utility beyond the core benchmarks.

Honest discussion of failure cases and limitations (engraved details, objects lacking clear part hierarchy, long-tail part distribution, lack of semantic labels), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline bootstraps from PartField's clustering outputs as pseudo-labels; since PartField itself is distilled from 2D SAM supervision, a substantial fraction of the claimed '5 million native 3D' labels are not fully independent of 2D-lifted supervision, which somewhat tempers the 'trained natively on 3D data' narrative for the majority of the training corpus (500k of the fully native 180k).

Table 2 comparisons for automatic segmentation handicap PartField by disabling mesh connectivity (replaced with K-means), while the PartSAM pipeline benefits from an optional graph-cut post-processing step using connectivity in the appendix (Table 4) that is not applied symmetrically to baselines; although the rationale (avoiding label leakage) is explained, the asymmetry in available post-processing could be discussed more thoroughly for a fully controlled comparison.

No evaluation of robustness to prompt ambiguity/multi-granularity consistency quantitatively beyond qualitative figures (e.g., no systematic study of how the three output tokens handle fine vs. coarse part ambiguity, which was central to SAM's own evaluation).

The semantic labeling limitation (masks without category labels) is acknowledged but not addressed experimentally, limiting applicability of claims around being a general 'foundation model for 3D part understanding' for tasks requiring semantics.

Training data construction relies on Objaverse(-XL) and proprietary/licensed datasets; full reproducibility of the curation pipeline and the resulting 5M-pair dataset for the community is unclear (e.g., whether data/code/model weights will be released), which could limit the paper's community impact despite strong claimed results.

Comparisons such as Table 2's baselines (PartSLIP, Find3D) seem to use fairly dated or weaker settings without extensive tuning discussion, and it would strengthen the paper to clarify whether baseline results are reproduced by the authors or taken from original papers, given the very large performance gaps reported (>20 IoU points).
